analysis.one_liner: Cuts corporate taxes, lets companies bring foreign profits home at a reduced rate, and pays tobacco growers to exit federal quota programs.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 251-178 and the Senate 69-17, and the President signed it into law on October 22, 2004, after a conference committee stripped out overtime protections and FDA tobacco regulation that the Senate had added.
analysis.plain_summary: To comply with a World Trade Organization ruling, the bill repealed an old export tax break and replaced it with a new deduction for income from manufacturing, construction, farming, and other production done in the United States. It also created a one-year window for companies to bring profits parked in foreign subsidiaries back to the U.S. at an effective tax rate of about 5.25%, and it rewrote many international tax rules in corporations' favor. A separate title ended the federal tobacco quota and price support program, paying quota holders $7 per pound and growers $3 per pound, funded by fees on tobacco companies.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. manufacturers, construction and engineering firms, and multinational corporations gain the most: a new deduction worth up to 9% of domestic production income and a one-year chance to repatriate foreign earnings at roughly a 5.25% rate. Tobacco quota holders and growers get government payments totaling billions of dollars to leave the quota system. Small businesses, farmers, timber owners, ethanol and biodiesel producers, film studios, racetrack owners, sports franchises, and private tax-collection agencies all received specific tax benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the repealed extraterritorial income exclusion with a deduction for up to 9% of qualified domestic production income, phased in from 3% in 2005 to 9% in 2010, and usable against the alternative minimum tax.
Limits the new deduction to 50% of the employer's W-2 wages, tying part of the tax benefit to domestic payroll.

Allows U.S. corporations to deduct 85% of dividends received from their controlled foreign corporations during a specified window, requiring reinvestment under an approved domestic plan — an effective federal rate of about 5.25% on repatriated profits.

Ends the tobacco quota and price support programs and directs transitional payments of $7 per pound to quota holders and $3 per pound to active growers, funded by assessments on tobacco manufacturers and importers.
Allows taxpayers to deduct state and local sales taxes in lieu of state income taxes for 2004 and 2005 — a benefit mainly for residents of states without an income tax.
Extends small-business expensing of up to $100,000 through 2008 and makes numerous targeted breaks for farmers, timber owners, film and television productions, railroads, and energy producers.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury absorbs the cost of the corporate deductions, the repatriation window, and the tobacco buyout, which the general taxpayer ultimately funds. Wages excluded from Social Security taxes under the stock-option provision reduce payroll tax receipts that fund Social Security and unemployment insurance. The Senate's overtime protections and FDA tobacco regulation were stripped in conference, so workers and tobacco-control advocates got neither.

drawbacks.text: The conference report dropped the Senate's provisions that would have barred new Labor Department rules exempting many salaried employees from overtime pay and prohibited the Secretary of Labor from exempting any employee earning under $23,660 a year, leaving the 2004 overtime regulations in place.

The bill repeals the foreign personal holding company rules, repeals subpart F rules on foreign base company shipping income, and lets international shipping corporations elect a per-ton tax instead of corporate income tax, reducing taxes on income earned offshore.

Wages from exercising incentive stock options and employee stock purchase plan stock are excluded from Social Security, unemployment, and railroad retirement taxes, shrinking the payroll tax base that funds those programs.

The conference report also dropped the Senate's Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act, which would have given the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products; the tobacco buyout ends the quota program but pays former quota holders out of manufacturer assessments rather than new revenue.
The repatriation window required companies to file a reinvestment plan, but the law set no enforceable hiring or investment standards beyond the deduction itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a genuine public-purpose trigger — a WTO ruling forced the repeal of the export tax exclusion — and the replacement deduction is partially tied to domestic wages, which is a real design feature favoring domestic employment. But the bulk of the act is business tax relief: the repatriation holiday, relaxed international tax rules, and dozens of targeted industry breaks were paid for out of federal revenue while workers' overtime protections and FDA tobacco regulation, both passed by the Senate, were cut in conference. On balance the law mainly served corporate and multinational interests, with the tobacco buyout and the sales tax deduction as the principal benefits flowing to individuals.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 251-178 in June, the Senate amended and passed it in July, and a conference committee's final version — which dropped the overtime and FDA tobacco provisions the Senate had added — cleared the House 280-141 and the Senate 69-17 in October before the President signed it.

narrative.text: The House Ways and Means Committee reported the bill 27-9 on June 14, 2004, and the House passed it on June 17 by a recorded vote of 251-178, with Republicans voting 203-23 for and Democrats 48-154 against.
Rep. Charles Rangel's motion to recommit — which would have replaced most of the bill's tax titles — failed 193-235, with 192 of 205 Democrats supporting it and no Republicans.

The Senate passed its own amended version by voice vote on July 15, 2004, adding overtime protections, restrictions on outsourcing federal work, FDA regulation of tobacco, and stronger tax shelter penalties.

House Democrats' motion to instruct conferees to keep domestic production tax relief, avoid new benefits for multinationals' overseas operations, and not increase the deficit failed 205-215 on September 29, with 200 of 205 Democrats in favor and all but 4 Republicans opposed.

The conference report, filed October 7, 2004, dropped the overtime and FDA tobacco provisions and set the domestic production deduction at 9% phased in from 2005, with the repatriation deduction capped at 85% of foreign dividends.
The House adopted the conference report 280-141 on October 7, the Senate invoked cloture 66-14 and passed it 69-17 on October 10-11, and it became Public Law 108-357 on October 22, 2004.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations gained the repatriation window and relaxed offshore tax rules; domestic manufacturers and construction firms gained the new deduction; tobacco quota holders and growers gained multi-year buyout payments. Workers lost the overtime protections and the public lost the FDA tobacco provisions the Senate had passed.

sides.party_line_note: House passage split sharply by party (Republicans 203-23 for, Democrats 48-154 against), while the Senate was more bipartisan: 25 of 48 Democrats joined 43 Republicans to pass the conference report 69-17.

industries.note: The bill lets companies deduct 85% of dividends from their foreign subsidiaries in a one-year window (an effective 5.25% rate) and repeals rules taxing offshore shipping income and foreign personal holding companies. The revenue cost falls on general taxpayers.

industries.industry: Domestic manufacturers, construction and engineering firms
industries.note: They gain a new deduction of up to 9% of domestic production income, capped at 50% of W-2 wages, which ties part of the benefit to domestic employment. The cost is borne by the Treasury rather than the industry.

Manufacturer and importer assessments fund the roughly $9.6 billion transition payments that end the quota and price support program, which had constrained leaf supply and pricing. Consumers see no price protection; the payments go to quota holders and growers.

Quota holders receive $7 per pound and active growers $3 per pound in transitional payments through FY 2014, with rights of survivorship — a direct government payment to a small group of asset owners.
Corporations operating ships internationally may elect a per-ton tax instead of standard corporate income tax, and subpart F rules on foreign base company shipping income are repealed.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, ethanol, and film industries
industries.note: The bill adds credits for marginal oil and gas wells, low-sulfur diesel, ethanol and biodiesel mixtures, expensing for film and television production, and capital-gains treatment for timber. These are targeted subsidies paid from general revenue.

industries.industry: Tax shelter promoters and advisory firms
industries.note: The bill imposes disclosure requirements on reportable transactions, penalties on promoters of abusive shelters of up to 50% of gross income from the activity, and expanded authority for the Treasury to enjoin shelter participants — strengthening enforcement against tax avoidance.

The bill authorizes Treasury to hire private collection agencies to collect unpaid taxes, letting agencies retain up to 25% of amounts collected and shielding the United States from liability for their acts.
